promptText: What is pgvector, in one sentence?
options: A standalone vector database that replaces PostgreSQL entirely
An open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds a native vector column type and ANN index types (IVFFlat, HNSW), letting Postgres store embeddings and run similarity search directly in SQL
A Java library for computing cosine similarity in application code
A managed cloud service exclusively offered by AWS
explanation: pgvector adds a native vector type and ANN index access methods to PostgreSQL, allowing similarity search to run as ordinary SQL inside the same database that already holds relational data.

promptText: Without any ANN index, is `ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector LIMIT 5` correct, and is it fast?
options: It is neither correct nor fast without an index
It is correct (an exact sequential scan computing distance to every row) but not fast, since it is linear in table size
It is fast but not correct, since it skips most rows
It cannot execute at all without an index
explanation: Without an index, PostgreSQL falls back to a sequential scan that computes distance against every row, which is exact but linear in table size -- correct but not scalable.

promptText: Which pgvector distance operator corresponds to cosine distance?
explanation: <=> is cosine distance, <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance, and <#> is negative inner product; each must match how the embedding model expects vectors to be compared.

promptText: In pgvector's IVFFlat index, what does the `lists` parameter control?
options: The number of query results returned per search
The fixed number of centroids/buckets that vectors are clustered into at build time via k-means
The number of database replicas maintaining the index
The maximum number of dimensions allowed in the vector column
explanation: IVFFlat clusters the table's vectors into `lists` centroids at build time; at query time, only the nearest few centroids' buckets (controlled by `probes`) are actually searched.

promptText: What is the basic mechanism HNSW uses in pgvector to answer similarity queries?
options: It sorts all rows by primary key and binary-searches for the closest vector
It builds a multi-layer graph connecting each vector to approximate neighbors, navigating from a sparse top layer to denser lower layers to converge on nearby vectors
It stores a pre-computed answer for every possible query vector
It requires a separate machine learning model to run at query time
explanation: HNSW builds a navigable multi-layer graph where a sparse top layer allows large jumps and denser lower layers refine the search, converging on an approximate answer without touching most nodes.

promptText: What happens if a query uses a distance operator (e.g., Euclidean `<->`) that doesn't match the operator class an index was built with (e.g., cosine `vector_cosine_ops`)?
options: PostgreSQL throws a clear compile-time error preventing the query from running
The query still runs and returns a result, but it silently doesn't use the index for that operator and may return a mathematically different ranking than intended
PostgreSQL automatically rebuilds the index using the new operator class
The query returns an empty result set
explanation: A mismatched operator does not throw an error -- it silently falls back to not using the index for acceleration and can return a different, potentially incorrect ranking, a failure mode with no obvious signal.

promptText: When would choosing pgvector over a dedicated vector database like Pinecone or Milvus be the wrong call?
options: Whenever the team already operates PostgreSQL for other data
When you need very high query throughput at very large scale, horizontal sharding of the vector index specifically, or would otherwise contend with primary OLTP workload on the same instance
Whenever vector search needs to be combined with a relational tenant filter
Whenever the dataset is under a few million vectors
explanation: pgvector is well-suited to moderate scale (hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of vectors) combined transactionally with relational data; past very large scale or very high throughput, a dedicated vector database's specialized architecture becomes the better fit.

promptText: A team bulk-loads two million new, semantically different document chunks into a table with an existing IVFFlat index and notices search quality drop. What is the most likely cause?
options: IVFFlat indexes automatically rebuild themselves after any bulk insert, so this shouldn't happen

The IVFFlat centroids were computed from the data distribution at index build time; a large new batch of semantically different content can leave those centroids poorly representative, degrading recall until the index is rebuilt
PostgreSQL silently drops the oldest vectors once a row limit is exceeded
HNSW indexes always degrade after bulk loads, but IVFFlat never does
explanation: IVFFlat's clustering reflects the data present at build time; a large new batch of different content can leave the original centroids poorly matched to the new distribution, silently hurting recall until the index is rebuilt.

promptText: Why is pgvector's ability to insert a document's metadata, content, and embedding in the same transaction hard to replicate with a separate dedicated vector database?
options: Dedicated vector databases don't support inserting any metadata alongside vectors

Replicating atomic multi-write consistency across two separate systems requires either a distributed transaction protocol (rarely supported, operationally painful) or an eventual-consistency pattern with a window where the two systems can disagree
It isn't actually hard; all vector databases support the same ACID transactions as PostgreSQL
Dedicated vector databases can only store one vector per table
explanation: A single BEGIN...COMMIT block in Postgres can atomically write a document's row and its embedding together; achieving the same guarantee across two separate systems requires distributed transactions or accepting an eventual-consistency window -- pgvector eliminates this class of bug by construction.

promptText: What is the trade-off of using `halfvec` instead of the default `vector` type for storing embeddings?
options: halfvec stores each dimension as a 2-byte half-precision float, roughly halving memory footprint, at the cost of a small loss of numeric precision that has negligible effect on nearest-neighbor ranking for most models
halfvec doubles storage but improves search recall
halfvec is only usable with the Euclidean distance operator
halfvec removes the need for an ANN index entirely
explanation: halfvec cuts per-dimension storage from 4 bytes to 2, which can be the deciding factor in whether an HNSW graph fits in shared_buffers at scale, with minimal practical impact on ranking quality since relative distance ordering is robust to small precision loss.

promptText: What is the difference between the maximum dimensions a `vector` column can store versus the maximum it can support with an ANN index built on it?
options: There is no difference; both limits are identical
A vector column can store up to 16,000 dimensions with no index; building an ANN index (IVFFlat or HNSW) on it caps out at 2,000 dimensions for `vector` (4,000 for `halfvec`)
The index limit is always higher than the storage-only limit
pgvector has no dimension limits of any kind
explanation: pgvector allows storing up to 16,000-dimension vectors without an index, but ANN index structures were designed around typical embedding sizes and cap indexable dimensions at 2,000 for vector (or 4,000 for halfvec, since each dimension costs half the bytes).

promptText: When checking `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output to confirm a vector query is using its ANN index, what should you look for?
options: A `Seq Scan` node, which indicates the index is being used efficiently
An `Index Scan` node referencing the vector index by name (e.g., using hnsw or ivfflat), as opposed to a `Seq Scan` node on the base table
The total number of columns returned by the query
The database's connection pool size at query time
explanation: An Index Scan node naming the HNSW or IVFFlat index confirms the ANN index is being used; a Seq Scan node instead indicates PostgreSQL is falling back to scanning the whole table, often due to an operator mismatch or small table size.

promptText: A query filters by a highly selective `tenant_id` and orders by vector distance in the same SQL statement. Why can the order in which PostgreSQL's planner applies the ANN index versus the tenant filter create a correctness risk, and how should this be verified?
options: There is no risk; PostgreSQL always applies filters before vector search

If the planner applies the ANN index first and filters by tenant afterward, the approximate nearest neighbors found before filtering may all belong to other tenants, returning fewer than k results or none -- this must be verified with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and potentially addressed with partial indexes or query restructuring
This risk only exists when using the Euclidean distance operator
The risk is eliminated automatically by adding a LIMIT clause
explanation: Depending on cost estimates, the planner might run the ANN search before applying a highly selective filter, and if the raw top-k results mostly belong to other tenants, the final filtered result set can be incomplete or empty -- staff-level engineers must confirm the actual plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and use partial indexes or query restructuring if needed.

promptText: Why might building an HNSW index over ten million rows require raising `maintenance_work_mem`, and what happens if it is left at a low default?
options: maintenance_work_mem only affects VACUUM operations, never index builds

Building an HNSW graph requires holding substantial working-set structure in memory; if maintenance_work_mem is too low, the build process spills intermediate state to disk and pages it back in repeatedly, potentially slowing a build from minutes to many hours
Raising maintenance_work_mem is purely cosmetic and has no effect on build time
maintenance_work_mem controls how many concurrent queries can run during the index build
explanation: HNSW index construction holds significant graph structure in memory; an inadequate maintenance_work_mem setting forces disk spillover during the build, which can turn a build that should take minutes into one taking many hours -- raising it for the build session (not necessarily globally) resolves this.

promptText: Why can't a single HNSW index serve both cosine-distance and Euclidean-distance queries equally well, and what must a team do if their application genuinely needs both?
options: A single index can serve both metrics equally well with no additional work required

The graph structure built by an operator class is shaped around that specific metric's notion of nearness, since cosine and Euclidean distance can disagree about which points are closest (especially for unnormalized vectors) -- serving both efficiently requires building two separate indexes on the same column
Switching between metrics only requires changing a session-level SET parameter, no rebuild needed
Euclidean distance queries can always reuse a cosine-distance index without any performance penalty
explanation: An operator class ties an index's internal structure to one specific distance metric's notion of nearness; since cosine and Euclidean distance can rank the same vectors differently (particularly when unnormalized), serving both well requires two separate indexes, doubling build time, storage, and maintenance cost.
